analysis.one_liner: Makes bad-faith corporate bankruptcies dismissable and ends liability caps that shield parent companies from injury claims.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended with 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change bankruptcy law to let courts throw out Chapter 11 filings made in bad faith or that serve no real reorganization purpose. It creates a presumption of bad faith when a company manufactures an artificial bankruptcy venue or restructured itself to shed liabilities, and it stops the bankruptcy automatic stay from protecting parent companies and other non-debtor entities facing injury claims like toxic exposure lawsuits affecting 100 or more people. In practice it targets the strategy of spinning off mass-tort liabilities into a separate subsidiary, sending it into bankruptcy, and capping what injured people and other creditors can collect.
analysis.who_benefits: People with injury or toxic-exposure claims against large companies (for example, workers and consumers with mesothelioma or talc-related claims) would be able to sue the solvent parent company even if a subsidiary filed for bankruptcy. Ordinary creditors would get more of what they are owed, and communities would keep more company value instead of seeing it drained by fees and strategic filings.

how_it_helps.text: Courts may dismiss a Chapter 11 case filed 'objectively futile' or in 'subjective bad faith', with the debtor bearing the burden of proof. [S2]

The court presumes bad faith if the debtor manufactured the venue, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence, and conclusively presumes bad faith for tactical litigation advantage, imposing delay on creditors, capping liability to protected creditors, a divisional merger within four years, insider asset transfers, or lacking a valid reorganizational purpose. [S2]

The bankruptcy automatic stay no longer blocks lawsuits against non-debtor entities, such as parent companies, on 'protected claims' arising from ownership, management, insurance, or corporate restructuring, or mass injury and contamination claims affecting at least 100 individuals. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations facing mass-tort or asbestos-style liability, and their parent companies, would lose the ability to cap their exposure by shifting liabilities into a bankruptcy filer. The restructuring industry built around these filings would lose business. Some companies with legitimate restructurings could face extra litigation and delay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mass-tort-exposed corporations and restructuring law firms

drawbacks.text: The conclusive presumptions are sweeping: any debtor restructured within four years, or whose filing caps liability to certain creditors, is automatically deemed to be acting in bad faith, which could sweep in legitimate restructurings that protect jobs and going-concern value. [S2]

A 'protected claim' is triggered by injury claims affecting as few as 100 individuals, a threshold that captures far more than the giant mass-tort cases the bill is aimed at, so mid-sized companies could face prolonged litigation against non-debtor affiliates during bankruptcy. [S2]
Mandating a 24-month timeline for plan proposals and making bad-faith dismissal easier could push marginal firms toward liquidation rather than reorganization, which can cost jobs. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the giant strategic filings the bill targets — spin a subsidiary with the liabilities, file in a favorable venue, cap the payout to injured people — the benefits to victims and creditors are substantial and the costs fall on shareholders and their advisers, who created the exposure. The main cost is that some ordinary restructurings of companies with modest liability would face more litigation and a tighter deadline, and a few might liquidate instead of reorganize. The bill could have been narrowed, but its core purpose addresses a real and documented channel through which solvent parents avoid paying injured people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the bill in the House on July 23, 2024, with Reps. Jerrold Nadler and Lance Gooden listed as original cosponsors. [S1, S2]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place. [S4]
The bill carried 2 cosponsors, one from each party, according to the cosponsor record. [S3]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so any bill not enacted expired. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that use spinoff bankruptcies to cap liability for injury and contamination claims, and the restructuring lawyers and advisers who run those filings, keep the current rules. Injured people and creditors left short in such cases are no better off.

for.name: Emilia Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought changes to bankruptcy law targeting bad-faith filings and non-debtor stays.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred, leaving it to expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny: one Democratic sponsor plus one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, and no committee or floor action ever occurred, so no recorded votes show the partisan shape.

industries.industry: Large corporations facing mass-tort liability (pharma, chemical, consumer products)
industries.note: The bill removes the automatic-stay shield for parent companies on injury and contamination claims affecting 100 or more people and presumes bad faith for debtors restructured to shed liabilities. Its gain — capped payouts — comes directly out of what injured people can collect.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy restructuring bar and advisory firms
industries.note: The lucrative practice of engineered spinoff bankruptcies in favorable venues would face presumptions of bad faith and mandatory dismissal grounds. The bill's cost lands on the firms that design and run these filings.

industries.industry: Private equity and corporate parent companies
industries.note: Non-debtor parents, owners, officers, and insurers could again be sued directly on claims tied to the debtor's conduct, ending a key protection for parent companies that keep assets out of the bankruptcy estate.
Bad-faith filings that impose delay and cap recoveries become dismissal grounds, and more company value stays available to pay what is owed.
